---
name: issue-absorption
description: Record and interpret issues absorbed by a Ticket. Use when publishing an absorbing Ticket, reading absorption records, or selecting absorbed issues for closing lines or closure.
user-invocable: false
---

# Issue absorption

This is a reference contract. Load it for the absorption decision, then continue the caller's workflow. Tracker reads, comments and closes use the project's configured tracker doc; this contract owns their meaning, not their commands.

## Write the agreement

- Read each source issue's body **and comments**. Put every requirement that must land with the fix into the Ticket's acceptance criteria, or into the Ticket that owns the file it touches.
- Name the issues the Ticket absorbs and link their briefs instead of copying them. Absorbed issues are linked sources, not parents: do not make the Ticket their sub-issue.
- For each source, put a separate `Closes #<n>` criterion in the Ticket's acceptance criteria. Once the Ticket exists, comment on each source: `Absorbed by #<ticket>; closes when it is completed.`
- Immediately before publication, re-read each absorbed issue's state and drop or note any already closed.

## Read the agreement

Read the source's comments and the absorbing Ticket's current state and close reason. The **latest** `Absorbed by` comment is authoritative: older records or criteria do not override it.

| Authoritative Ticket | Meaning for its source issues |
| --- | --- |
| Open | Waiting on this Ticket; keep the sources open. |
| Closed as completed | The fix completed; the sources may close with this Ticket. |
| Closed any other way (not planned, duplicate, abandoned) | Not fixed; the sources stay available to planning with their votes. They are neither waiting on the Ticket nor evidence of a failed completed fix. |

A later absorption record transfers this agreement to its named Ticket. Unrelated issues have no absorption agreement. Callers still own recurrence checks, planning verdicts, user approval and when to perform a close.

## Closing lines and closure

The pull request completing a Ticket carries a separate `Closes #<n>` line for each source it authoritatively absorbs. Include only sources of Tickets that the pull request actually completes; recheck the latest records when maintaining those lines. A dropped or never-landed Ticket cannot authorize closing its sources. Retain a source's line only when a Ticket the pull request completes is its authoritative absorber.

Before closing a source with a Ticket, recheck that the authoritative Ticket is closed as completed. Otherwise leave the source open and apply the state table. A source becoming eligible for closure does not bypass the caller's approval or recurrence policy.
---
name: retro-planning
description: Work through this repo's Retro backlog: snapshot the open Retro issues, group them by root cause, walk the user through each group one at a time and act on each call at once (a Ticket, a close, or a spin-off to its own planning), keeping an open record that is closed at the end. Use when Retro planning is due, or to resume one whose record is still open.
---

A **Retro planning** works through one repo's **Retro backlog** (its open issues labelled `retro`): it merges duplicates, closes one-offs, and turns repeated problems into Tickets. Run this thread at the **premium** tier: the snapshot, verdict, cap, order, spin-off and expiry rules below interact, and each must be applied exactly.

Plan only the current repo. Its tracker is named in `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`; with no such file, use the GitHub repo of the checkout's `origin` remote. Read and write only that repo's issues, using the commands that file gives.

**The cap: at most 3 Tickets per planning.** Every Ticket this planning files counts toward it: repeated groups, severe one-offs and failed fixes alike. A spun-off group does not count. Only the user may raise the cap, and only for this planning: when more groups qualify than fit, say so, and keep the cap unless the user raises it. The record notes the cap used and the user's reason.

Load `issue-absorption` before reconciling absorption records, classifying the snapshot or carrying out an absorption or close-with-Ticket verdict. Apply its agreement and lifecycle as reference while continuing this planning.

If the brief says this thread owns a spun-off group, skip steps 0 to 7 and go straight to "Running a spun-off planning".

## 0. Resume or start

Look for an open issue labelled `retro-planning`. If there is one, this is a resumed planning, and its creation time stays the snapshot time:

1. If its Snapshot section is still "None", continue at step 1.
2. Otherwise read its snapshot table and cap, then reconcile the record with each snapshot issue's current state: closed, an `Absorbed by` comment made since the snapshot, a `Spun off to` comment, or a Ticket labelled `ready-for-agent` filed since the snapshot that links it and is not named in a spin-off's `Filed #<ticket> (from spin-off` comment. Any call carried out on the issues but missing from the record goes into the record now, so no group is walked twice and no Ticket filed twice. An issue with a `Spun off to` comment belongs to its spin-off: record only the spin-off itself, if the record lacks it, and leave its later closes and Tickets to the spin-off's comments.
3. Reconcile any unfinished handoff before walking another group: search for already-created Tickets even if labels or absorption comments are missing, using the recorded identifiers, source links and approved work. Count each real Ticket once toward the cap, and resume `to-tickets` with its existing identifiers, mappings, solution approval and incomplete actions to repair publication rather than create it again. Preserve a declined solution and the user's problem verdict; resume the pending decision, not a fresh proposal.
4. Redo steps 2 to 4 on the snapshot issues that still have no verdict, counting the record's "Tickets filed" toward the cap, then continue at step 5.

Otherwise file the record now as an **open** issue (format in "The record", with Cap `3 (default)` and every other section "None" for now), creating the `retro` and `retro-planning` labels if the repo lacks them. Its creation time is the **snapshot** time.

Done when there is exactly one open record and you know whether this planning is resumed.

## 1. Read the snapshot and the earlier records

The snapshot is everything filed or commented before the record's creation time, and it is all this planning plans. An issue filed, or a `Seen again` comment made, after that time **arrived during this planning**: leave it for the next planning, and list it in the record at step 7. Other threads keep running meanwhile; nothing is held.

- Every open issue labelled `retro` in the snapshot, with its body, comments and creation date.
- Every **closed** issue labelled `retro-planning` (the earlier records, format below), newest first. From them take: the groups the newest record held back by the cap, every Ticket in its "Tickets filed" and every Ticket in its `Filed #<ticket> (from spin-off ...)` comments, each with the Retro issues it absorbed, and each open issue's "plannings without a new vote" count from the newest record.

Count each issue's **votes by distinct thread**: the thread its body names as the source, plus the thread of each `Seen again in <thread link>` comment in the snapshot. A thread counts once, however many comments it left. An issue has a **new vote** when it was filed, or got a `Seen again` comment, after the newest closed record was created; with no record yet, every issue has one.

Give each issue a status:

- **Waiting on an open Ticket**: the absorption contract says waiting. List it, and leave it out of steps 2 to 5.
- **Spun off, waiting**: it has a `Spun off to <thread link>` comment and no later `Absorbed by` comment. Its owning planning has not decided it yet. List it, and leave it out of steps 2 to 5.
- **Failed-fix candidate**: the absorption contract says completed, with a new vote since the Ticket closed. It goes to step 2.
- **Closing with its Ticket**: the contract says completed, with no new vote since. Its verdict is **Close with its Ticket**.
- **In the backlog**: every other issue, including the contract's not-fixed sources. Keep its votes and new-vote answer, and group and judge it in steps 2 to 5 like any other.

Write the snapshot table into the record.

Done when every open `retro` issue in the snapshot has its distinct-thread count, its new-vote yes or no, and its status, and the record holds them.

## 2. Recheck earlier fixes

For each Ticket named in an earlier record that closed as completed, check whether its problem has come back: an absorbed issue with a new vote after the Ticket closed, or a Retro issue in the snapshot filed or voted on after it closed that matches the Ticket's problem. Each match makes a **failed-fix group**: the fix did not work. This runs before the cap is filled, and a failed-fix group counts toward it.

Apply the absorption contract to mark the other closed Tickets "not fixed".

Done when every closed Ticket in the earlier records is marked "holding", "came back" or "not fixed", with the matching issues.

## 3. Group and propose verdicts

Group the remaining backlog issues by root cause and merge duplicates. A group's vote count is the number of distinct threads across all its issues, so one thread that filed two duplicates counts once.

Give each group the first verdict that fits:

1. **Act, failed fix**: a failed-fix group from step 2.
2. **Expire**: the group has had no new vote across 2 plannings. That is: every issue in it has a count of 1 or more under "plannings without a new vote" in the newest record, and none has a new vote. Close it with "reopen if seen again". A group the newest record held back by the cap never expires.
3. **Act**: seen in 2 or more distinct threads.
4. **Act, severe**: seen in one thread, but severe: lost data, a security problem, or a large waste of time or money.
5. **Close as `wontfix`**: seen in one thread and not severe. Write the reason.

Done when every group, and every issue closing with its Ticket, has a verdict, and every `wontfix` a reason.

## 4. Order the walk

Order the acting groups:

1. Failed fixes.
2. Groups the newest record held back by the cap.
3. The rest, by distinct-thread count, highest first; on a tie, the group with the oldest issue first.

After them come the `wontfix` groups, oldest issue first. Expiries and issues closing with their completed Ticket are the **mechanical closes**: they leave no judgment to make and wait for the end of step 5.

Done when every group has its place in one ordered walk.

## 5. Walk the user through each group, one at a time

Take the groups in the step 4 order. While this planning has filed fewer Tickets than the cap allows (spin-off Tickets live only in comments on the record and do not count), the next acting group is proposed as a Ticket; once the cap is full, each later acting group is shown as **held back by the cap**. So when the user closes or spins off a proposed Ticket, its slot stays free and the next acting group moves up into it.

Show one group, with full details:

- **Background**: how the skill or workflow works today, at the point the issues touch.
- **What went wrong**: the concrete incident in each thread that filed or voted on it.
- **Root cause** the issues share, and the distinct-thread count.
- **Proposed verdict** with its reason.
- For an acting group: the intended outcome and whether to address this problem. Ticket preparation follows that call.

Then ask for the user's call and wait for it: address the problem, spin off, close, or the user's own change (a different verdict, a reshaped problem, keep it open). Approval to address a problem authorizes preparation, not its concrete solution. Record the call, carry it out at once with step 6, and reconcile the result in the record before showing the next group. A call that changes the grouping regroups only the groups not yet walked.

When every group is walked, show the mechanical closes in one short list (each issue, and the completed Ticket that absorbed it, or "expired"), and carry them out once the user agrees. One the user holds back stays open.

Done when every group in the walk and every mechanical close has the user's call, carried out and in the record.

## 6. Carry out a call

- **Address the problem**: invoke the complete `to-tickets` workflow. Pass the intended outcome; source reports explicitly marked as issues to absorb; agreed constraints, failed-fix context and known dependencies; this one group's scope; and the remaining actual-ticket budget. Request one complete Ticket, with a return before publication if investigation requires several. Prefer a mechanical check or hook over a prose rule; pass that preference as a constraint, with a reason required when only prose can address the problem. `to-tickets` owns context gathering, investigation, drafting, tier/dependency discussion, concrete-solution approval and verified publication. Include any existing publication identifiers, source mappings, approval and incomplete actions on resume.
  - Reconcile its returned identifiers, source-to-ticket mappings and incomplete actions into the record. A real Ticket counts immediately even when a later label, link, comment or verification failed. Keep the handoff pending and resume its unfinished actions before showing another group; never recreate an existing Ticket.
  - If several Tickets are necessary, return to the user's spin-off decision before any publication. Keep the cap unchanged unless the user explicitly changes it; a larger budget alone does not turn this one-Ticket handoff into permission to publish several.
  - If the solution is declined, preserve both the problem approval and solution rejection, with the user's next call (revise, spin off, close or keep open). A decline creates no Ticket and consumes no slot. Once a solution has been approved and published, update the record without asking for solution approval again.
- **`wontfix`** or another close: comment the reason, add the `wontfix` label (the string `docs/agents/triage-labels.md` maps it to, if the repo has that file) when the verdict is `wontfix`, and close.
- **Spin off**: the group needs more discussion, so this planning does not decide it. Ask for a separate planning thread for its issues: in a project with a coordinator, ask the coordinator; otherwise tell the user to start one, and give them the brief. The brief names the issues, this record, and "Running a spun-off planning" below. On each issue, comment `Spun off to <thread link>; that planning decides it.` (with no link yet, name the thread as the user or coordinator named it). A spun-off group stays open, does not count toward the cap, and cannot expire.
- **Expire**: comment `No new vote across 2 plannings. Reopen if seen again.` and close.
- **Close with its Ticket**: recheck eligibility under `issue-absorption`; when eligible, comment `Closed with #<ticket>.` and close, otherwise apply its current lifecycle state.
- **Held back by the cap**, or kept open: leave open.

Then update the record straight away: the group's row in "Verdicts", its line in "Tickets filed", "Held back by the cap" or "Spun off", and "Cap" when the user raised the cap. Keep pending handoffs in "Incomplete actions", including the problem verdict, solution approval or rejection, published identifiers, source mappings and remaining work; clear that entry only after reconciliation.

Done when the issue's state matches the call and the record shows it.

## 7. Close the record

End every planning by closing the record, also when the user declined every verdict: once closed, it is the newest record, so `retro`'s clock runs from its creation (the snapshot time) and the expiry counts advance. Before closing, fill "Arrived during this planning" (each open `retro` issue filed, and each `Seen again` comment made, after the snapshot time), "Open issues: plannings without a new vote", and the waiting lists. Then close it, and give the user its link.

A planning that pauses before the end leaves its record open; the next run of this skill resumes it at step 0.

Done when the record is complete and closed, and the user has its link.

## Running a spun-off planning

When the brief says this thread owns a spun-off group, plan only its issues with the user. Discuss them as long as the user needs, then give each issue a verdict, carried out as in step 6: absorbed by Tickets prepared and published through the complete `to-tickets` workflow, or closed with a reason. Pass this spun-off scope and its agreed budget instead of the ordinary one-Ticket limit; the originating planning's cap does not apply here. File no `retro-planning` record of your own, and never edit the body of the record that spun it off: its planning is the body's only writer. Instead, comment on that record, open or closed: right after filing each Ticket, one comment for it, `Filed #<ticket> (from spin-off <this thread's link>), absorbs #<n>, ...`, so later plannings recheck it in step 2, and one more listing each issue you closed with its reason. The thread's work is done when no issue it owns is left open without an `Absorbed by` comment, and every Ticket it filed has its `Filed` comment on that record. On resuming this thread, first check that every Ticket it filed has its `Filed` comment, and post any that is missing.

## The record

An issue titled `Retro planning <yyyy-mm-dd>` (the snapshot's date), labelled `retro-planning`. It is open while the planning runs and closed at its end; the next planning reads only closed records, so each section below is required, with "None" when empty:

```markdown
Snapshot time: <the record's creation time>

## Cap

3 (default) / <n>, raised by the user: <reason>

## Snapshot

| Retro issue | Distinct threads | New vote | Status |
|-------------|------------------|----------|--------|
| #12 | 2 | yes | in the backlog |
| #18 | 1 | no | waiting on #35 |
| #19 | 1 | no | spun off, waiting |

## Verdicts

| Group | Retro issues | Distinct threads | Verdict | Reason or Ticket |
|-------|--------------|------------------|---------|------------------|
| <root cause> | #12, #15 | 3 | Ticket | #40 |
| <root cause> | #13 | 1 | wontfix | <reason> |
| <root cause> | #14 | 2 | held back by the cap | |
| <root cause> | #20 | 2 | spun off | <thread link> |
| <root cause> | #16 | 1 | kept open by the user | |
| absorbed by a Ticket closed as completed | #11 | 2 | closed with its Ticket | #31 |

## Incomplete actions

None / <group: problem verdict; solution decision; existing Ticket identifiers and source mappings; remaining actions>

## Held back by the cap

- <root cause>: #14

## Tickets filed

- #40 (<root cause>), absorbs #12, #15

## Spun off

- <root cause>: #20, owned by <thread link>

## Earlier fixes rechecked

- #31: holding / came back (#17) / not fixed

## Arrived during this planning

- #22 filed
- #14 seen again in <thread link>

## Open issues: plannings without a new vote

- #14: 0
- #16: 1

## Waiting on open Tickets

- #18: #35

## Spun off, waiting

- #19: <thread link>
```

Every verdict appears, kept-open ones included. "Plannings without a new vote" covers every snapshot issue left open that is not waiting on a Ticket or spun off: 0 if it had a new vote since the previous record or is held back by the cap, otherwise the previous record's count plus 1 (a missing count is 0). "Spun off, waiting" lists issues spun off by an earlier planning and still undecided; this planning's own spin-offs are under "Spun off".

# Fixture issue tracker
This repository uses only Markdown files under issues/ as its tracker. Read full files including comments. Each issue has State, Labels and Created lines. New issue: next unused number filename, with its issue body and metadata. Append comments under Comments. Edit state to close. Read files to verify writes. Native dependencies and parents are unavailable: use Blocked by and Part of body lines when needed. Source briefs link as issues/<number>.md. No remote tools or real tracker actions. No build is authorized; this is planning only.
State roles: ready-for-agent, needs-triage, needs-info, ready-for-human, wontfix. Category: bug, enhancement. No agent-only mapping.

name: to-tickets
description: "Split a plan, spec or conversation into tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring what blocks it, and publish them to the tracker. Use when the user says \"break this into tickets\" or \"split into issues\", or asks for vertical slices of an existing spec."
---

# To Tickets

Break a plan, spec, or conversation into a set of **tickets**: tracer-bullet vertical slices, each declaring the tickets that **block** it.

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `setup-dev-skills`.

## Process

### 1. Gather context

Work from whatever is already in the conversation context. If the user passes a reference (a spec path, an issue number or URL) as an argument, fetch it and read its full body and comments.

When another workflow calls this skill, retain its intended outcome, source roles (absorbed reports versus a parent), scope, constraints, failed-fix context, dependencies and publication budget. A problem approval permits investigation; step 4 still obtains approval of the concrete work. Load `issue-absorption` now when sources will be absorbed, so their bodies and comments inform the draft.

For a resumed publication, first reconcile existing identifiers and source mappings with tracker state, including Tickets whose labels or links were never completed. Retain the prior solution decision and repair only incomplete actions. An existing Ticket is not a new publication slot.

### 2. Explore the codebase (optional)

If you have not already explored the codebase, do so to understand the current state of the code. Start at `docs/index.md` and open only the docs that fit (with no index, fall back to `GLOSSARY.md` or `GLOSSARY-MAP.md`, and `docs/adr/`). Ticket titles and descriptions should use the project's domain glossary vocabulary, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

Look for opportunities to prefactor the code to make the implementation easier. "Make the change easy, then make the easy change."

### 3. Draft vertical slices

Break the work into **tracer bullet** tickets.

<vertical-slice-rules>

- Each slice cuts a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests): vertical, NOT a horizontal slice of one layer
- A completed slice is demoable or verifiable on its own
- Each slice is sized to fit in a single fresh context window
- Any prefactoring should be done first

</vertical-slice-rules>

Give each ticket its **blocking edges**: the other tickets that must complete before it can start. A ticket with no blockers can start immediately.

Give each ticket a **model tier**, the tier its Implementer runs on: **regular** by default, **premium** for heavy or tricky work (a subtle design call, wide-reaching changes, concurrency, security or money logic). Name the tier, never a vendor's model.

**Wide refactors are the exception to vertical slicing.** A **wide refactor** is one mechanical change (rename a column, retype a shared symbol) whose **blast radius** fans across the whole codebase, so a single edit breaks thousands of call sites at once and no vertical slice can land green. Don't force it into a tracer bullet; sequence it as **expand–contract**. First expand: add the new form beside the old so nothing breaks. Then migrate the call sites over in batches sized by blast radius (per package, per directory), each batch its own ticket blocked by the expand, keeping CI green batch to batch because the old form still exists. Finally contract: delete the old form once no caller remains, in a ticket blocked by every migrate batch. When even the batches can't stay green alone, keep the sequence but let them share an integration branch that all block a final integrate-and-verify ticket; green is promised only there.

For a caller requesting one complete Ticket, return before publication if the work needs several: explain the required slices and why one would be oversized, and let the caller settle the larger scope. Respect its available budget; a cap is not permission to expand the requested scope.

### 4. Quiz the user

Present the proposed breakdown as a numbered list. For each ticket, show:

- **Title**: short descriptive name
- **Blocked by**: which other tickets (if any) must complete first
- **Model tier**: regular or premium, and for premium one line on why
- **What it delivers**: the end-to-end behaviour this ticket makes work

Ask the user:

- Does the granularity feel right? (too coarse / too fine)
- Are the blocking edges correct: does each ticket only depend on tickets that genuinely gate it?
- Should any tickets be merged or split further?
- Does each ticket's model tier fit its difficulty?

Iterate until the user approves the concrete breakdown. If the user declines, publish nothing; return the rejection and any next decision to the caller. On resume, retain an existing solution approval unless the proposed work changes.

### 5. Publish the tickets to the configured tracker

Publish the approved tickets. **How** depends on the tracker `setup-dev-skills` configured; the tickets are the same either way, only the shape of the blocking edges changes:

- **Local files** → write one file per ticket under `.scratch/<feature-slug>/issues/<NN>-<slug>.md`, numbered from `01` in dependency order (blockers first). Each file's "Blocked by" lists the numbers/titles it depends on. Use the per-ticket file template below: one ticket per file, never a single combined file.
- **A real issue tracker (GitHub, Linear, …)** → publish one issue per ticket in dependency order (blockers first) so each ticket's blocking edges can reference real identifiers. Use the platform's native blocking relationship where it has one; otherwise write each ticket's blockers in the form the tracker doc reads (for GitHub without native dependencies, a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line as the first line of the ticket body, above everything else including a `Part of #<parent>` line, and no `## Blocked by` section). The tracker doc's form wins over the issue template's `## Blocked by` section. If a native write fails at run time (for example a server without the dependencies API), write the tracker doc's fallback form for that ticket instead, using the tracker doc's way of adding a line to an issue body (the ticket already exists, and rewriting its body without reading it first loses its text), listing every blocker of that ticket, not only the failed one. Then check with the tracker doc's way of counting open blockers (it reads both the native edge and the body line) that every blocker of the ticket is in place in one form or the other; do not report the ticket published until they are. When blockers are written as the tracker doc's `Blocked by:` line or set as native edges, omit the `## Blocked by` section, including for a ticket with no blockers; write "None (can start immediately)" only where the template section is kept (local files). If the source was an existing issue that the tickets split (a parent, not one a Ticket absorbs, see below), make each ticket its sub-issue (tracker doc's operation). If that write fails at run time (for example a repo without sub-issues enabled), write the tracker doc's fallback form for that ticket instead, again with the tracker doc's way of adding a line to an issue body (a `Part of #<parent>` line on the line after the `Blocked by:` line, or as the first line if the ticket has none); then check with the tracker doc's way of checking a sub-issue link (it reads both the sub-issue edge and the body line) that the ticket is linked in one form or the other, and do not report the ticket published until it is. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label unless instructed otherwise; the tickets are agent-grabbable by construction. If the repo has a release doc (`docs/agents/release.md`) that defines a label prefix, and the source issue carries a label with that prefix (its Release's label), give each ticket that label too, so a Spec's Tickets ship in its Release. If the repo's triage-labels doc (`docs/agents/triage-labels.md`) maps an agent-only role to labels, and the source issue carries one, give each ticket that same label too, so the agent that the Spec is for builds its Tickets; when the source issue carries none, give no ticket one. Give no other ticket a release label: an issue filed during a Release waits for the next Release planning.

If the source is **one or more existing issues** that a Ticket absorbs, load `issue-absorption` and apply its writing agreement while drafting and publishing. Right before publishing, also re-read every blocker's state and drop or note any already closed.

Work the **frontier**: any ticket whose blockers are all done. For a purely linear chain that means top to bottom.

Do NOT close or modify any parent issue.

**Model tier:** this ticket's tier as agreed with the user: `regular` or `premium`.

**Model tier:** this ticket's tier as agreed with the user: `regular` or `premium`.

## Acceptance criteria

</issue-template>

In either form, avoid specific file paths or code snippets: they go stale fast. Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts, not a working demo, just the important bits.

### 6. Offer `setup-project`

Once the tickets are published, decide whether they changed what the project's threads need: a new repo, a new kind of thread, or a new standing rule. If so, offer the user `setup-project` in one line naming what changed. Only offer: call the Skill tool with "setup-project" only after the user says yes. If nothing changed, say nothing about it.

### 7. Return to the caller

Return the outcome (published, needs larger scope, declined or incomplete), every created Ticket identifier, source-to-ticket mappings, and all unfinished actions. Preserve identifiers even if creation succeeded but a later operation failed; report those as incomplete rather than fully published. The caller reconciles its record and cap before continuing. Do not ask again for an unchanged solution's approval on return.
